title: India Just Made the Four-Day Workweek Legal. Here's What It Actually Means for NRIs Thinking About Moving Back.
excerpt: The new labour codes allow companies to offer three days off per week — with a catch. For the millions of diaspora professionals weighing a return to India, the fine print matters more than the headline.
body:
India's new labour codes, now fully operational after years of legislative limbo, include a provision that would have seemed fantastical a decade ago: companies can legally offer their employees a four-day workweek with three consecutive days off. The catch — and there is always a catch — is that the 48-hour weekly cap remains untouched. Four days of work means 12-hour shifts.

The Code on Wages (Central) Rules, notified on May 8, consolidate 29 colonial-era and post-independence labour laws into four streamlined codes covering wages, industrial relations, social security, and occupational safety. The four-day option is the provision that has captured headlines, but the overhaul is far more sweeping — and for NRIs considering a return to India, the entire package reshapes the calculus.

## The Fine Print on Four Days

Under the new framework, an employer may compress the standard workweek from five or six days into four, provided total weekly hours do not exceed 48 and the arrangement is not imposed unilaterally. Employees must consent. Any work beyond scheduled hours triggers overtime compensation at double the regular wage rate. Mandatory rest intervals and break periods still apply within each shift.

The model is expected to gain traction first in sectors where output is measured by deliverables rather than hours: information technology, IT-enabled services, global capability centres, consulting, design, and marketing. India's IT services industry, which employs over five million people and has been grappling with return-to-office mandates since 2024, is the obvious testing ground. Manufacturing, healthcare, logistics, and hospitality — industries bound by shift rotations and physical presence requirements — will find adoption far more difficult.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For the estimated 18 million Indians living abroad, work culture has long been one of the stickiest barriers to return. The six-day workweek that still prevails across much of Indian industry, the expectation of long hours without proportionate compensation, and the absence of formal protections for flexible work have made "moving back" a lifestyle downgrade for many professionals accustomed to Western labour norms.

The new codes do not magically transform Indian workplaces. A legal option is not a cultural norm, and the gap between what the law permits and what employers actually offer has historically been vast in India. But the signal matters. For the first time, Indian labour law explicitly accommodates compressed schedules, codifies overtime protections at the central level, and mandates written employment contracts — a basic safeguard that was absent for a startling number of workers.

The reforms also address two pain points that disproportionately affect returning NRIs. First, basic pay must now constitute at least 50 percent of total compensation, which restructures the take-home-versus-benefits equation that many returnees find opaque. Second, the five-year vesting period for gratuity has been abolished, meaning shorter stints at Indian companies are no longer penalized.

## The Bigger Picture

Prime Minister Modi has added fuel to the flexible-work conversation. Speaking amid surging crude oil prices driven by the Iran crisis — with Brent crude touching $126 per barrel — Modi called on companies to revive work-from-home practices adopted during the pandemic. "We had become accustomed to them," he said, framing remote work as a matter of national energy security rather than employee preference.

The juxtaposition is telling. India's labour reform is arriving not as an idealistic experiment in work-life balance but as a pragmatic response to converging pressures: a competitive global talent market, an energy crisis that makes commuting expensive, and an IT industry that risks losing its best people to companies and countries that already offer flexibility.

## What Remains Uncertain

Implementation will be the test. The central codes set the framework, but state governments must adopt them — and India's states have historically moved at different speeds on labour reform. Companies operating across multiple states will fall under the central framework, which provides some uniformity, but enforcement capacity varies enormously.

For NRIs watching from abroad, the four-day workweek headline is less important than the broader trajectory: India is modernizing its labour architecture, and the direction is toward flexibility, formalization, and worker consent. Whether that trajectory holds will depend on whether Indian industry treats the new codes as a floor to build on or a ceiling to bump against.
